properties.name: Hydrate from document to first query, measured across five design sizes with NO database and NO index: 1,000 nodes = 270 ms, 3,140 nodes = 8.8 s. Cost is superlinear in EDGES (~627 µs/edge at the top vs 143 at the bottom) and 95% of it is import_graph, not JSON parsing and not the store
properties.statement:
THE MEASUREMENT `dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants` ASKED FOR ON 2026-08-09 — *"the one measurement worth taking now, while nothing depends on the answer: hydrate-and-index time as a function of design size (200 / 2k / 20k nodes, import to first query)"*. Taken 2026-08-24, at Anthony's instruction, on reflow2's own design at main `1ef45e5`.

METHOD: `cargo test --release -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` — **release build, in-memory backend, NO RocksDB and NO tantivy**. Parse the export, open a `DesignGraph`, `import_graph`, then a typed scan as the first real query. Sub-sampled documents take the first N nodes and only the edges whose BOTH endpoints survive.

    nodes   edges    parse    import    TOTAL to queryable    µs/edge
      200       0    6.0ms     6.8ms         27.7 ms             —
      500     409   22.9ms    58.7ms         93.8 ms            143
     1000    1247   47.0ms   205.3ms        270.0 ms            165
     2000    4318  127.8ms  1136.7ms       1279.6 ms            263
     3140   13390  385.6ms  8397.6ms       8827.9 ms            627

⭐⭐ THE HEADLINE, AND IT REDIRECTS THE WHOLE QUESTION: **THE BYTE STORE IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK, BECAUSE THERE IS NO BYTE STORE IN THIS MEASUREMENT.** No RocksDB, no redb, no disk — and the top-end hydrate is still 8.8 seconds. JSON parsing is 386 ms of it (4%); opening the graph is 34 ms; the first query is 11 ms. **`import_graph` is 8,398 ms — 95% of the total.** Choosing a different embedded engine cannot move this number, and neither can dropping the engine entirely.

⭐ THE COST IS SUPERLINEAR IN EDGES, NOT IN NODES. Per-edge cost RISES from 143 µs to 627 µs as the graph grows — a 4.4x degradation. Between the last two points, edges grow 3.1x and time grows 7.4x, an exponent near 1.8; between the middle two, near 1.5. Consistent with adjacency lists being read-modify-write on every edge insert, so each edge into a high-degree node rewrites that node's whole list, and average degree climbs with density (3,140 nodes carry 13,390 edges, and hub nodes like `proj:reflow2` carry far more than the 8.5 average). **That is an implementation property of the import path, not a fact about storage architecture, and it is optimisable — batching adjacency writes is the obvious first move.**

⇒ WHAT IT MEANS FOR DOCUMENT-AS-TRUTH, stated at the altitude the decision needs: **a typical design hydrates comfortably.** 1,000 nodes in 270 ms and 500 in 94 ms are both far inside the "under a second and it is routine engineering" bar the 2026-08-09 node set. reflow2's OWN design is the pathological case, and it is pathological because it is the biggest and densest design that exists anywhere — no tenant of a hosted tier would look like it. So the model is viable today for the sizes it would actually serve, AND it degrades badly enough with growth that the import path would need work before anybody leaned on it.

🛑 BOUNDS — THIS IS A LOWER BOUND, NOT THE FULL COST. **The full-text index was OFF.** A real hydrate that must answer `search_design` also has to build the tantivy index, which is not in any number above. The 200-node row has ZERO edges (an artifact of sub-sampling by node prefix) so it measures node-only import and must not be read as a 200-node design. Single machine, single run per size, no warm-up, debug of the OS page cache uncontrolled. The 20k-node point the original request asked for was not taken — no design that large exists to sample.

📌 FOR CONTRAST, the same hydrate INTO RocksDB with fulltext ON, debug build: 96–134 s, producing a 12–13 MB store. Not comparable to the table above (different build profile and different feature set) and recorded only so nobody mistakes one for the other.
